scenes.headline: Partitioning
scenes.subtitle: Physically organize data for partition pruning
scenes.narration: Partitioning splits a table's data into directories by column values so queries can prune irrelevant data.

scenes.headline: How partitioning works
items: Data is stored in folders per partition value
Filters on the partition column prune whole directories
Best for low-cardinality columns like date or region
scenes.narration: Each distinct partition value gets its own directory of files. A query filtering on that column skips entire directories it does not need. This works best when the column has relatively few distinct values.

scenes.headline: Creating a partitioned table
scenes.code:
CREATE TABLE web_logs (
  event_id STRING,
  user_id STRING,
  payload STRING,
  event_date DATE
)
USING DELTA
PARTITIONED BY (event_date);
scenes.narration: This table is physically split by event date on disk. A query with a date filter reads only the matching partitions. Choosing the right partition column is the key decision here.

scenes.headline: Good vs bad partition keys
scenes.narration: A good partition key has few distinct values and appears in most query filters. A high-cardinality key like user id explodes into countless tiny directories and hurts performance. Balance is essential to avoid skew and file sprawl.

scenes.headline: Common pitfalls
items: Over-partitioning creates the small files problem
On modern tables, liquid clustering often replaces it
scenes.narration: Too many partitions fragment data into inefficient tiny files. Partitioning by a high-cardinality column is a classic mistake that degrades queries. For new tables, liquid clustering now often supersedes manual partitioning.

scenes.text: Partition on what you filter, keep cardinality low, and avoid tiny fragments.
scenes.narration: The right partition strategy turns a full-table scan into a quick, targeted read.
